properties.description: Pure consciousness, witness, uncaused, non-productive.
Root nature, uncaused cause of the material universe.
Illumination, lightness, pleasure.
Activity, motion, pain.
Restraint, heaviness, indifference.
Intellect, determination.
Ego-sense, individuation.
Mind, internal organ of synthesis.
The Internal Instrument
The Subtle Body
Means of valid knowledge.
The mind-field (Buddhi, Ahamkara, Manas combined)
Special Purusha untouched by afflictions
The 8 Limbs of Yoga
Absolute Independence
The fundamental instruments or sources through which accurate, valid knowledge (pramā) of the world is acquired. Nyaya accepts four: Perception, Inference, Analogy, and Verbal Testimony.
Direct, unmediated knowledge arising from the contact (sannikarsha) of a sense organ with its object. It must be non-erroneous, determinate, and not dependent on verbal cognition.

Cognition that follows a prior perception. It is the logical deduction of an unperceived object (like fire) based on the perception of a logical sign or mark (like smoke), relying on the memory of their invariable concomitance (vyapti).

Knowledge of the relationship between a name and the object it denotes, based on a recognized similarity to a familiar object (e.g., identifying a wild gavaya because one was told it looks like a cow).
The instructive assertion of a reliable, trustworthy authority (Apta). It provides valid knowledge regarding both perceptible things (worldly facts) and imperceptible things (spiritual realms).
A person who has direct, accurate knowledge of a subject, is devoid of prejudices or motives to deceive, and communicates clearly out of compassion or a sense of duty.
The established, historical agreement within a community that a specific word denotes a specific object or meaning.
The ultimate corpus of spiritual and ritual knowledge in Indian philosophy, considered valid because they are the testimony of supreme Aptas (ancient seers or God).
A direct prescriptive statement or command in a text urging the listener to perform a specific action to achieve a specific result.
Sentences that provide praise, blame, historical context, or mythological backing to support and motivate the performance of a primary Injunction (Vidhi).
The repetition of a previously stated command or concept for the sake of emphasis, clarification, or instructional continuity.

nodes.label: पूर्वपक्ष (pūrvapakṣa) - Prima Facie View / Opponent's Objection

properties.description: The initial argument, counter-claim, or skeptical objection presented against an established doctrine.
The final, proven doctrinal truth established after thoroughly refuting the opponent's view (Purvapaksha) using valid means of knowledge.
The eternal, immaterial substance that is the substratum of consciousness, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain.
The atomic, internal sense organ that mediates between the eternal soul and the external senses. It can only process one cognition at a time.
The physical and cognitive connection between a sense organ (like the eye) and its corresponding object (like color) that triggers direct perception.
A distinct, unified substance that comes into existence when its parts (avayava) combine. A pot is not just a pile of clay atoms; it is a new entity: 'The Whole'.
The eternal, all-pervading substance that causes our cognitions of past, present, and future, and acts as the universal container for all actions.
A conflicting judgment regarding the exact character of an object, arising from the perception of properties common to many objects.

The sixteen topics of inquiry outlined by Gautama: means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, doubt, purpose, familiar instance, established tenet, members of a syllogism, confutation, ascertainment, discussion, wrangling, cavil, fallacies, quibbling, futile rejoinders, and clinchers.
The critical investigation and testing of a subject that has been defined.
The causal chain leading from false knowledge to suffering, and its reversal leading to liberation.
The apprehension or apprehension-producing activity that illuminates objects.
Mutually exclusive statements about the same object, leading to doubt.
Irregularity in apprehension or non-apprehension, leading to doubt.
A debate where both parties sincerely aim to discover the truth, establishing their own position using pramāṇas and logic.
That which is to be known through pramāṇas. The objects of knowledge.

nodes.label: ?????? ?????? (dvada?a prameya) - The Twelve Objects of Knowledge

properties.description: The twelve specific objects of knowledge: Soul, Body, Senses, Objects of Senses, Intellect, Mind, Activity, Fault, Transmigration, Fruit, Pain, and Liberation.
Synonymous with knowledge and apprehension in the Nyaya system.
A process of reasoning that assists in knowing the true nature of a thing by revealing the absurdities of contrary suppositions.
The physical architecture of interaction: the body is the site of experience, the senses are the instruments, and the material elements are their objects.
An undisputed example that both ordinary people and experts agree upon.
A logical fallacy where a proposition requires an infinite series of justifications, without ever reaching a foundational grounding.
The core components of the karmic cycle: Faults (attachment, aversion) drive Activity (speech, mind, body), which inevitably produce a Fruit (experience of pleasure or pain).
A 'pseudo-probans'. A reason (hetu) that appears to be valid but is actually defective and fails to establish the conclusion.
Absolute deliverance from pain. The state of the soul freed from the cycle of birth, activity, and fault.
A logical fallacy where the reason (hetu) exists both where the probandum (sadhya) exists and where it does not.
The objective or motive that induces someone to act or engage in a discussion.
A meaningful arrangement of words. In Nyaya, it refers specifically to the statements of an authoritative person (apta).
The five members of a formal inference used to convince others: Proposition, Reason, Example, Application, and Conclusion.
The opposition to a statement by assigning to it an unintended meaning.
An objection based on mere similarity or dissimilarity, without addressing the underlying logical connection.
The point in a debate where a participant is defeated due to a contradiction, evasion, or inability to grasp the opponent's point.
An analogy explaining how a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) validates itself while validating an object, just as a lamp illuminates itself while illuminating a room.
The critical investigation into the existence, nature, and eternal status of the self (ātman) as distinct from the body, senses, and mind.
The doctrine that the soul (ātman) is uncreated and indestructible, existing continuously across different bodies through transmigration.
The principle that senses operate by physically reaching or coming into direct contact with their objects (e.g., visual rays traveling to the object).
The critical investigation of cognition or intellect (buddhi), establishing it as a temporary quality of the soul rather than an eternal substance.
The Buddhist doctrine that all entities exist only for a single instant before ceasing to be, completely replaced by a new entity in the next instant.
The invisible moral force or latent potential generated by past actions (karma) that determines future experiences and the initial formation of the universe.
The operation of speech, mind, and body, driven by desire or aversion, which initiates the cycle of karma and rebirth.
The underlying psychological flaws—attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa), and delusion (moha)—that compel a person to act.
The strong attraction or desire for objects that yield pleasure, leading to continued bondage and repeated activity.
The strong repulsion or hatred toward objects or situations that yield pain, driving aggressive or avoidance behaviors.
The fundamental ignorance or misconception of reality, primarily mistaking the non-self (body/mind) for the self.
The cycle of dying and being born again in a new physical body, driven by the accumulated merit and demerit of past actions.
Any physical, verbal, or mental action that generates an unseen moral consequence (adṛṣṭa) affecting the agent's future.
The Buddhist Madhyamaka theory that all things are fundamentally empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature or independent existence.
The supreme, eternal soul who creates, sustains, and destroys the universe, and who dispenses the fruits of karma to individual souls.
The materialist view that the universe and living beings emerge purely by random chance without any intelligent cause or moral design.
The assertion that absolutely everything in existence is temporary and subject to destruction.
That which is uncreated, indestructible, and exists forever without modification (e.g., souls, atoms, ether).
That which is produced and eventually destroyed; any composite object made of parts.
The view that everything that exists is permanent, and change is merely an illusion or a shift in manifestation (often associated with strict Advaita or Sāmkhya).
The extreme pluralist view that every entity is entirely isolated and distinct, denying any real unifying categories or universals.
The extreme nihilist view that nothing truly exists at all.
The experiential result (pleasure or pain) of one's past actions, representing the fruition of karma.
A concept primarily from Mīmāṃsā, representing the unseen intermediary force generated by a ritual that brings about a future result.
The fundamental nature of worldly existence; the physical and psychological pain inevitably linked to birth and attachment.
The ultimate release from the cycle of rebirth and suffering, synonymous with Apavarga.
The accurate, direct realization of the true nature of the sixteen categories (padārthas) and the distinction between the soul and non-soul.
The false identification of the true self (ātman) with the physical body, mind, or senses.
The mental resolve or intentionality that precedes physical or verbal action.
The eternal, indivisible, infinitesimal building block of the physical universe in Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika ontology.
The state of deep, undisturbed concentration on the true nature of the soul.
The continuous, disciplined repetition of philosophical reflection and meditation.
The practical methods of mental and physical control used to focus the mind.
The foundational ethical disciplines (like non-violence and truthfulness) required to purify the mind.
The constructive personal disciplines (like study and purity) that support spiritual growth.
A sincere discussion with teachers or peers aimed purely at discovering the truth, without the desire to defeat the other.
A debate where the primary goal is victory over the opponent rather than the discovery of truth, using any logical means necessary.
A form of debate where the participant only attacks the opponent's thesis without establishing any thesis of their own.

Supreme felicity (Release/Moksha) is attained by the knowledge of the true nature of sixteen categories: Means of Right Knowledge (Pramana), Objects of Right Knowledge (Prameya), Doubt (Samsaya), Purpose (Prayojana), Familiar Instance (Dristanta), Established Tenet (Siddhanta), Members of a Syllogism (Avayava), Confutation (Tarka), Ascertainment (Nirnaya), Discussion (Vada), Wrangling (Jalpa), Cavil (Vitanda), Fallacy (Hetvabhasa), Quibble (Chhala), Futility (Jati), and Point of Defeat (Nigrahasthana).
Pain, birth, activity, defect, and misapprehension; on the successive annihilation of these in the reverse order, there follows Release (Apavarga).
Perception (Pratyaksha), Inference (Anumana), Comparison (Upamana), and Verbal Testimony (Shabda) are the means of right knowledge (Pramanas).
Perception is that knowledge which arises from the contact of a sense organ with its object, and which is determinate, unnameable (not associated with a mere name), and non-erratic (infallible).
Inference is knowledge which is preceded by perception, and is of three kinds: a priori (Purvavat), a posteriori (Sesavat), and commonly seen (Samanyatodrsta).
Comparison is the knowledge of a thing through its similarity to another thing previously well known.
Verbal Testimony (Word) is the instructive assertion of a reliable person (Apta).
It (Verbal Testimony) is of two kinds: that which refers to matter which is seen, and that which refers to matter which is not seen.

Soul (Atman), Body (Sharira), Senses (Indriya), Objects of sense (Artha), Intellect (Buddhi), Mind (Manas), Activity (Pravritti), Fault (Dosha), Transmigration (Pretyabhava), Fruit (Phala), Pain (Dukha), and Release (Apavarga) are the objects of right knowledge (Prameya).
Desire, aversion, volition, pleasure, pain, and intelligence are the marks (indicators) of the Soul.
The body is the site of gesture (action), senses, and sentiments (pleasure and pain).
The senses are the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear; they are produced from the elements.
The elements are earth, water, light (fire), air, and ether.
Smell, taste, color, touch, and sound are the objects of the senses, and are qualities of the earth, etc., respectively.
Intellect (Buddhi), apprehension, and knowledge—these are non-different (synonymous).
The mark of the mind (Manas) is that there do not arise in the soul more acts of knowledge than one at a time.
Activity (Pravritti) is that which makes the voice, mind, and body begin their action.
Faults (Dosha) have the characteristic of causing activity.
Transmigration (Pretyabhava) is rebirth.
Fruit (Phala) is the thing produced by activity and faults.
Pain (Dukha) is that which has the characteristic of causing uneasiness or affliction.
Release (Apavarga) is the absolute deliverance from pain.

Doubt (Samsaya) is a conflicting judgment about the exact character of an object, arising from the recognition of properties common to many objects, from properties not common to any, from conflicting testimony, and from irregularity of perception and non-perception.
Purpose (Prayojana) is that with an eye to which one proceeds to act.
A familiar instance (Drishtanta) is that thing about which an ordinary man and an expert entertain the same opinion.
An established tenet (Siddhanta) is a dogma resting on the authority of a certain school, hypothesis, or implication.
The dogma of all schools, a dogma peculiar to some school, a hypothetical dogma, and an implied dogma—these are the four kinds of established tenets.
A dogma of all the schools is a tenet which is not opposed by any school and is claimed by at least one school.
A dogma peculiar to some school is a tenet which is accepted by similar schools, but rejected by opposite schools.
A hypothetical dogma is a tenet which, if accepted, leads to the acceptance of another tenet.
An implied dogma is a tenet which is not explicitly declared as such, but which logically follows from the examination of particulars concerning it.
The members (Avayava) of a syllogism are Proposition (Pratijna), Reason (Hetu), Example (Udaharana), Application (Upanaya), and Conclusion (Nigamana).
A Proposition (Pratijna) is the declaration of what is to be established.
The Reason (Hetu) is the means for establishing what is to be established, derived from the similarity of the case in hand to the example.
Also, from its dissimilarity to the example.
An Example (Udaharana) is a familiar instance which, through its similarity to what is to be established, is possessed of the property of that which is to be established.
Or, through its dissimilarity, it is destitute of that property.
Application (Upanaya) is the winding up, with reference to the example, of what is to be established as being so or not so.
Conclusion (Nigamana) is the restating of the proposition after the reason has been mentioned.
Confutation (Tarka) is a reasoning which, for the purpose of ascertaining the real nature of a thing of which the character is not known, shows the absurdity of all contrary characters.
Ascertainment (Nirnaya) is the determination of the real character of a thing, after having pondered over two conflicting parties, by means of consideration of the thesis and the antithesis.

Discussion (Vada) consists in the defending of a thesis and an antithesis by means of proofs and reasonings—a defense not opposed to established tenets, carried on by five members, and resulting in the ascertainment of the truth.

Wrangling (Jalpa) is that which is endowed with the said characteristics, but is also characterized by the defending of one's own position by means of quibbles, futilities, and processes worthy of rebuke.
Cavil (Vitanda) is that (wrangling) which is devoid of the establishing of one's own position.
Fallacies of reason (Hetvabhasa) are the erratic (Savyabhicara), the contradictory (Viruddha), the equal to the question (Prakaranasama), the unproved (Sadhyasama), and the mistimed (Kalatita).
The erratic reason (Savyabhicara) is one which is not restricted to one end.
The contradictory reason (Viruddha) is one which opposes an established tenet.
The reason equal to the question (Prakaranasama) is one which is put forward to establish a definite conclusion, but leaves the question in its original state of doubt.
The unproved reason (Sadhyasama) is one which needs to be proved in the same way as the proposition.
The mistimed reason (Kalatita) is one which is adduced when the time in which it might hold good has passed.
Quibble (Chhala) is the opposition offered to a proposition by the assumption of an alternative meaning.
It is of three kinds: quibble in respect of a term (Vak-chhala), quibble in respect of a genus (Samanya-chhala), and quibble in respect of a metaphor (Upacara-chhala).
Quibble in respect of a term consists in wilfully taking a term in a sense other than that intended by the speaker, when the term happens to be ambiguous.
Quibble in respect of a genus consists in asserting the impossibility of a thing by transferring the attribute of a species to its genus.
Quibble in respect of a metaphor consists in denying the truth of a statement by taking it in its literal sense when it was used in a metaphorical sense.
[Objection] Quibble in respect of a metaphor is not different from quibble in respect of a term, because it does not differ from it in being an alternative meaning.
[Reply] No, because they are different in character.
If there were no difference between them, there would be only one kind of quibble.
Futility (Jati) is an objection based on mere similarity and dissimilarity.
A Point of Defeat (Nigrahasthana) arises when one misunderstands, or does not understand at all.
Since there are many kinds of futilities and points of defeat, they are manifold.

(Objection): If it is said that doubt arises from the apprehension of common and peculiar properties, from conflicting views, and from irregularity in apprehension and non-apprehension, we say no; there is no doubt, because it depends on another object (the specific property).
(Objection continued): And because of the apprehension of the object as it actually exists.
(Objection continued): (Doubt) is un-ascertained knowledge, but it would be possible (only) if there were causes for ascertainment.
(Objection continued): And in the case of conflicting testimony, there is (actually) an agreement (or conviction).
(Objection continued): And because irregularity is regular in its own nature of being irregular.
(Objection continued): And thus there would be endless doubt, because the property (causing it) is continuous.

(Gautama's Reply): Doubt arises precisely from the apprehension of the (common) properties as stated, accompanied by the expectation of specific differences; therefore, it is neither the case that there is no doubt, nor that there is endless doubt.
(Reply continued): Wherever there is doubt, there is the continuous application of this same method (of critical examination).
(Skeptical Objection): Perception and the other (Means of Knowledge) are invalid, because they cannot be established in any of the three times (past, present, or future).
(Objection continued): If the Means of Knowledge (Pramāṇa) is established *before* (the object), then Perception cannot arise from the contact of the sense organ with the object.
(Objection continued): If it is established *after* (the object), then the object of knowledge (Prameya) is not established by the Means of Knowledge.
(Objection continued): If they are established *simultaneously*, since each cognition is restricted to its specific object, there would be an absence of sequential order in cognitions.
(Gautama's Reply): There is no valid denial (of the Pramāṇas), because the denial itself cannot be established in the three times.
(Reply continued): And because of the denial of all Means of Knowledge, the denial itself is unestablished.
(Reply continued): Or, if that (the denial) is valid, then it is not the case that all Means of Knowledge are denied.
(Reply continued): And the denial based on the three times is invalid, because they (the Pramāṇas) are established just as a musical instrument is established by its sound.
(Reply continued): And (a Pramāṇa) can become an object of knowledge (Prameya), just like a weighing scale.
(Objection): (The Pramāṇas cannot be established by other Pramāṇas) because that would lead to non-apprehension (due to infinite regress).
(Objection continued): Or, if that (infinite regress) is avoided, then the object of knowledge would be established just as the Means of Knowledge is established (without another Pramāṇa).
(Gautama's Final Reply): No, their establishment is just like the establishment of the light of a lamp.
(Objection): The definition of perception (given in Book 1) is untenable, because it is an incomplete statement.
(Reply): Perception does not arise in the absence of contact between the soul and the mind.
(Objection): In that case, there would be the contingency (of having to mention) direction, place, time, and ether as well.
(Reply): The soul is not excluded, because knowledge is its distinguishing mark.
(Reply): The mind is not excluded, because the non-simultaneity of those (cognitions) is its distinguishing mark.
(Reply): And the contact of the sense organ and the object is mentioned by its own specific words, because it is the specific cause of perception.
(Reply continued): And because, in the case of persons who are asleep or whose minds are distracted, (perception) is caused by the contact of the sense organ and the object.
(Reply continued): And specific cognitions are designated by them (the senses and objects).
(Objection regarding sleep): (The objection that sleeping people would perceive everything) is not a valid reason, because it is self-contradictory.
(Objection): Perception is (actually) inference, because the apprehension (of the object) is from grasping only a part.
(Reply): No, because there is perception of at least that much (the part).
(Objection): Since the 'whole' (avayavin) is yet to be proved, there is doubt regarding it.
(Reply): If the whole is not established, there would be non-apprehension of everything.
(Reply continued): And because holding and pulling are possible.
(Objection): If it is said that it is apprehended like an army or a forest; (Reply): We say no, because atoms are imperceptible.
(Objection): Inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is fallible (ambiguous), due to obstruction, destruction, and similarity.
(Reply): No, because there is a distinct difference in the objects from (mere) localized obstruction, fear, and similarity.
(Objection): The present time does not exist, because when a thing is falling, only the time that has been fallen through (past) and the time to be fallen through (future) are logically possible.
(Reply): If the present time does not exist, the other two (past and future) also cannot exist, because they are dependent upon it.
(Reply continued): The establishment of the past and the future is not based on their mutual dependence on each other.
(Reply continued): If the present does not exist, there would be non-apprehension of everything, because perception would be impossible.
(Reply continued): But the apprehension (of the present) is established in both ways, because of the possibility of what has been done and what is to be done.
(Objection): Analogy (Upamāna) is unestablished, because similarity may be complete, considerable, or partial.
(Reply): Analogy is established on the basis of a well-known similarity, so the stated defect does not arise.
(Objection): (Analogy is just Inference), because it establishes the imperceptible by means of the perceptible.
(Reply): We do not see the purpose of Analogy being fulfilled while the gavaya remains imperceptible.
(Reply continued): And because Analogy is established by the conclusive application 'so it is' (this is that), it is not non-different (from Inference).
(Objection): Word/Verbal Testimony (Śabda) is Inference, because the object is inferred from its inseparable connection (with the word).
(Objection continued): Because the apprehension does not operate in two different ways.
(Objection continued): And because of the relationship.
(Reply): The comprehension of the object from the word arises from the force of the instruction of a reliable person.
(Reply continued): And there is no (natural) relationship (between word and object), because filling, burning, and cutting are impossible.
(Objection): There is no denial (of a relationship), because there is a fixed determination of words and their meanings.
(Reply): No, because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is conventional.
(Reply continued): And because there is no uniformity (of meaning) among different groups of people.
(Objection): It (the Veda) is invalid, because it is tainted by the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
(Reply): No, (the failure is) due to defects in the action, the performer, or the materials.
(Reply continued): (There is no contradiction), because the statement of fault applies when there is a difference in the time of adopting (the alternatives).
(Reply continued): And because of the justification of re-inculcation (anuvāda).
(Reply continued): And because the meaning is comprehended from the classification of sentences.
(The classification is) into Injunction (Vidhi), Explanatory Assertion (Arthavāda), and Re-inculcation (Anuvāda).
Injunction (Vidhi) is that which enjoins (urges an action).
Explanatory Assertion (Arthavāda) consists of Praise, Blame, the actions of others, and Historical accounts.
Re-inculcation (Anuvāda) is the repetition of what has been enjoined by an injunction.
(Objection): There is no difference between Re-inculcation and Tautology, because both involve the repetition of words.
(Reply): It is not without a difference, because the repetition has a purpose, like the instruction 'go faster'.
(Conclusion): The validity of the Veda is established by the reliability of the trustworthy authority, just like the validity of incantations (mantra) and medical science (Āyurveda).
(Objection): There is no soul distinct from the senses, because sight and touch grasp one and the same object.
Not so, because of the fixed correspondence of each sense to its own object (sight to colour, touch to texture).
It is precisely because of this restriction of each sense to its own object that the existence of the soul is not to be denied.

(Objection): There is no soul distinct from the body, because there is no sin in burning the body (if the soul were separate and unharmed, burning a corpse should be no crime, yet cremating a living body is murder).

There would be no such crime even in the case of burning what is animated by a soul (i.e., a living body), on the assumption that the soul is eternal (since the eternal soul survives unharmed either way).
Not so, because it constitutes the killing of the agent who is the possessor and user of the effect (the body).
(A further, related question): Is there one visual sense or two, given that what is seen by one eye is recognized by the other (as the same object)?

(Objection): Not so, because it is not the case that we perceive a sense of doubling when an object is placed between the nose and a bone (i.e., between the two eyes) -- if there were truly two separate visual senses we should see everything doubled.
There is no unity, because when one (eye) is destroyed, the second is not destroyed (with it) -- so it is not one.
(Objection): There is no reason (for this conclusion), since even when a part is destroyed, the whole (organ) may still be apprehended to persist (as with a body missing a limb).
There is no valid objection here, because of the disanalogy with the illustrative case.
(A further point): Because of the alteration observed in relation to a different sense organ (e.g. squinting or eye-strain affecting only one eye at a time shows their independence).

(Objection continued): Not so, because memory has as its object only what has previously been experienced (so recognizing the same object with the other eye may just be a case of memory, not proof of a single sense).
There is no valid objection, because of the existence in the soul of the quality (that makes recognition, not mere organ-unity, the explanation).
(Objection): There is no soul distinct from the mind, because the causes that lead us to affirm a soul (desire, cognition, etc.) could equally well belong to the mind.
This is merely a difference of name, since it is established that the knower requires an instrument of knowing (so 'mind' as instrument is distinct from the 'soul' as the knower who uses it).

And the rule (that only one act of knowledge can occur at a time, established earlier as mind's own mark) is itself without any further inference behind it (i.e., it is a directly established, independent fact, not derivable from the mind being the soul).
(In favour of the soul's eternality/persistence across births): A newborn infant's experience of joy, fear, and grief is due to the operation of memory-impressions previously acquired.
(Objection): This is merely like the opening and closing (of petals) observed in a lotus and similar plants, occurring on their own (without needing prior memory).
Not so, because the five kinds of bodily reactions (of the lotus etc.) are caused by heat, cold, rain, and season, whereas (the infant's emotional reactions are not of this kind).
(Further evidence): from the infant's desire for the mother's breast, which arises from the practice/habituation of feeding in a former life.
(Objection): This might instead be like the movement of iron toward a magnet (a case of natural attraction requiring no memory at all).

Not so, because there is no such [comparable, undirected] activity toward anything else (an infant seeks specifically the breast for feeding, not indiscriminately anything nearby, as a purely mechanical attraction would predict).
Because we do not observe anyone born entirely free of passions (raga) [supporting that dispositions carry over from birth].
(Objection): This might arise the way a substance is produced together with its qualities (i.e., passions might simply co-arise naturally with the newly formed body, needing no prior-life source).
Not so, because passions like attachment (raga) etc. arise from mental resolve/intention (sankalpa) as their proximate cause, not automatically from mere bodily origination.
(One view): The body is (purely) earthy, because of the perception of an additional quality (smell, the distinctive quality of earth) in it.
The body is earthy-and-watery, because a quality of water (i.e. fluidity/moisture, such as sweat) is also perceived in it.
(Objection): It is made of four elements, because of the perception of inhalation and exhalation (indicating air) [in addition to earth and water, and implicitly heat].

(Objection continued): It is made of all five elements, on account of smell, moistness, digestion/cooking, formation of cavities, and provision of space -- all pointing to earth, water, fire, air, and ether respectively.
And also because of the authority of scripture (which describes the body as composed of the five elements).

There is doubt (about the nature of the visual sense), because we perceive things when they are present in contact with black collyrium (kajal, applied close to the eye) and also perceive things at a distance, separate from the eye.

(A Samkhya-style objection, seeking to deny visual apprehension of large vs. minute objects as evidence either way): Because both a large object and a minute (subtle) object are grasped (equally by the eye, contact-theory cannot explain the difference in how they're seen).
The seizing of that (visual object) is due to a specific contact of rays (of light/vision) with the object.
(Objection): There is no valid reason here, since such rays are never actually perceived (reaching out to the object).
It is not the case that non-perception (of a postulated cause) by direct sight is a valid reason for denying it, when that thing is (itself established) by inference.
And (specific contact is required) because of the observed difference according to the distinguishing feature of the object being perceived by its own particular substance-quality-relation.

The perception of colour/form occurs due to a combination inhering in several substances together with the specific character of the colour (i.e. colour-perception depends jointly on the object's colour-quality and its material composition).
And the arrangement/deployment of the senses, being effected by (past) action (karma), serves the purposes of the soul (purusha).

(Objection, re-raising the aprapyakaritva/non-contact view): Because we do not perceive the light of a torch (visible in the sky) at midday, (contact must be irrelevant; rather, sufficient light/visibility conditions matter, not literal touching).

Not so, because we also fail to perceive it at night (under different conditions where the torch-light itself is the dominant illumination, yet a different explanation is needed for daytime specifically).

Non-perception (of the torch by day) occurs because the object's manifestation is not achieved, owing to the object's dependence on assistance from external light (the torch's own faint light is overwhelmed by the much brighter ambient daylight).
And in the case where it does manifest (i.e., is bright enough to be seen), that occurs precisely because it overcomes (the competing brightness).
And also because of the observed visual rays of night-prowling animals (such as cats, whose eyes appear to shine/glow in the dark, evidencing the reality of ray-based vision).
(Objection, re-opened): Non-contact grasping (aprapya-grahana) is indicated, because of the perception of objects screened by glass, mica-sheets, and crystal.
There is no valid objection, given the observed non-perception of an object screened by a wall (which IS opaque, unlike glass/crystal).
Because there is no obstruction (in transparent media), the occurrence of contact (of the visual ray with the object) is established.
This is confirmed by the analogous case of the sun's rays, which, even when screened by crystal, are not obstructed in their power to burn (a combustible object placed behind the crystal).

(Objection): This would entail the undesired consequence of a mutual transfer of properties between the two objects (the burning object's heat-quality would need to belong reciprocally to the crystal itself, absurdly).
Just as with a mirror or clear water, visual perception (of reflected objects) occurs owing to the natural clarity/transparency (of the surface), (without any illegitimate property-transfer).

For, in the case of things established by direct observation as well as by inference, there is no scope for arbitrarily accepting or rejecting them (piecemeal) -- (the contact theory, established by both, must be accepted consistently).
There is doubt (as to whether the senses are one or many), because of the difference in their locations, and because (on a rival view) the whole (organ) is not confined to different locations.

(Objection, for a single sense = touch as the basis of all): Because it (the sense of touch) is not distinct from the body as a whole (the entire skin covers the body, so 'touch' might be the one underlying, all-pervasive sense).
Not so, because there is no simultaneous apprehension of (different) objects (if all senses were really touch, we should apprehend colour, sound, taste etc. all equally by touching, which we don't).

And, moreover, because of a direct contradiction (a monist claim of both single-sense and clearly-differentiated-sense-experience cannot both hold), touch cannot be considered a single, all-encompassing sense.
Because of the fivefold nature of the sense-objects (smell, taste, colour, touch, sound each being irreducibly distinct kinds of object).

(Objection): Not so, because there is a plurality even WITHIN each of these object-kinds (e.g. many different smells, many different colours) -- so the fivefold-object argument proves too much or too little.
There is no valid objection here, because smell-ness and the like (the underlying GENERIC quality-type) remain undivided across their many particular instances.

(Objection continued): Since there is no difference in respect of mere 'being-an-object' (of sense) as such, there should be (only) oneness (of the sense faculty, treating all sensory objects under one general category).
Not so, because of the fivefold distinction in respect of the seat/locus of cognition, its access-point, its mode of approach/movement, its characteristic form, and its generic type.
There is an essential identity (of each sense with its respective element), owing to the perception of the specific quality belonging to that particular element.
Of smell, taste, colour, touch, and sound, earth possesses (qualities) up to and including touch (i.e., earth has smell, taste, colour, and touch, but not sound).

(Objection, proposing the standard cumulative hierarchy): Water, fire, and air each progressively lack the immediately preceding element's distinguishing quality, with ether possessing the topmost/last quality alone (sound).
Not so, because we do not perceive all these qualities (in each of the intervening elements as claimed).

(Objection maintaining the hierarchy): Because of the singular, individual absence of the higher quality (i.e., the later, higher qualities are simply imperceptible in the lower elements, not truly absent), the higher elements' qualities remain imperceptible in the lower ones (in due sequence).
For, indeed, each subsequent (element) is pervaded/qualified by the preceding one.
Not so, because earth and water (specifically) are directly perceptible (in their distinguishing qualities, without needing this pervasion theory to explain their perceptibility).
Each element is regarded as 'principal/predominant' (with respect to a given quality) owing to the pre-eminence of the quality specifically distinctive of it.
That predominance, moreover, is established by the abundance/preponderance (of the relevant quality-instances in that element).
Because the (elements) possessing the (relevant) qualities are what constitute the (basis of the corresponding) sense organs.

And because that (element specifically) is not apprehended by that (corresponding sense) alone (implying the qualities of other, non-dominant elements are grasped through other means, not directly via the paired sense) -- this needs clarification and confirms the specific-pairing doctrine.

(Objection, raised by an opponent emphasizing sound's distinct status): Not so, because we (also) perceive the quality of sound (which does not fit neatly into this earth-through-air elemental scheme tied to the tangible senses).

That perception (of sound) is accounted for by the mutual difference in substance and quality between (ether and) the other elements (sound being ether's own distinctive quality, on exactly the same principle as smell for earth, etc.).
(Objection): There is doubt about cognition (buddhi), owing to its resemblance to action (karma) and to space/ether (akasha) -- i.e., is it eternal like ether, or non-eternal like action?

(In favour of non-eternality): Because of the recognition of an object (as the same object across successive cognitions, implying each cognition is a distinct, momentary event that must then be linked by something else).

(Objection to this reasoning): This is a case of an unproved reason (sadhya-sama), (since the recurring character used as evidence is exactly what's in question -- whether it implies real non-eternality or just successive manifestation of one thing).

Not so, because there is no apprehension of two cognitions occurring simultaneously (unlike the case of sound, where different manifestation-events of the eternal type were compatible with each other).
And if it (the earlier cognition) were not recognized (as continuing), it would entail the undesired consequence of complete destruction (of that cognition, further confirming non-eternality).
Because of its sequential occurrence, cognition is apprehended non-simultaneously (i.e., one at a time, in strict succession).

And the failure to recognize (an object via an earlier cognition, once attention has moved) is because of the mind's engagement with a different object (i.e., not because the earlier cognition persisted unrecognized, but because it has genuinely ceased and the mind has moved on).
(A rival, eternalist-leaning suggestion): Not so, because there is no (real) movement/transition (of the cognizing agent's engagement between objects, if buddhi belonged to something changeless).

(Reply): It is like the mistaken notion of 'otherness' one might form regarding a crystal (seen through different colored backgrounds) -- (the apparent multiplicity of transitions is a case of superimposition, not proof against non-eternality).

(A further, more radical view -- momentariness, associated with Buddhist thought): Just as with the crystal, there is a fresh arising of ever-new (successive states) even within a seemingly single continuous thing, owing to (its) momentariness, so this applies to (all apparent) individuals.

(A weaker fallback): In the absence of any (further) determining cause (either way), acceptance (of continuity or momentariness) simply follows how things appear (to ordinary perception, i.e., we should default to the common-sense view of persisting things).

Not so, because the causes of origination and destruction (of things) ARE, in fact, perceived (in ordinary experience, providing a real basis for the persisting-substance view against pure momentariness).

Just as, in the case of milk, the non-perception of any (specific observed) cause of its destruction (when it turns to curd, we only see cause of curd's origination, not literally milk's destruction) -- similarly this pattern of origination (of new states from continuous substance, not sheer momentary discreteness) holds.
Because it (the prior state) is grasped through inferential signs (linga), there is no (real problem of) non-perception (regarding the causal connection between the states).
Not (does the milk's disappearance occur) through (literal) transformation (in the momentariness sense), but through the arising of a different quality (in what remains one continuous substance).
The perception of a different arrangement/configuration (of parts, in the arising of a new substance) is the (proper basis for) inference of the cessation of the prior substance.

In some cases the cause of destruction is perceived, and in other cases it is not; hence there is no single, universal rule (governing all cases) -- (so a blanket doctrine of universal momentariness cannot be sustained).
(Returning to buddhi): It is not a quality of the sense organs or their objects, because cognition persists (in the form of memory) even after the destruction of the sense-object (contact).

And also because there is no simultaneous cognition (of multiple things at once, which rules out mind -- manas -- as the sole locus in the relevant sense, since mind is what accounts for exactly this non-simultaneity, distinguishing the locus of buddhi from a merely instrumental role).
That (non-simultaneity argument) would apply equally (even if cognition were held to be a quality of the soul, so it does not, by itself, decide the issue in favor of a different substrate).

(Objection, proposing the senses jointly as the substrate): Because of the absence of contact between the senses and mind (there being no direct link established, mind cannot properly transmit cognition to/from a further substrate like the soul).

Not so, because no (specific, additional) cause for such contact needs to be separately specified (contact-relations of this kind are already established through the general theory of substance-conjunction).
And because, if it (a settled cognition) persisted unchanged, there would be the undesired consequence of its being eternal (which cognition plainly is not, as established in the opening section).

The destruction of one cognition by another cognition (in succession) is exactly parallel to the case of sound (destroyed/succeeded by another sound-manifestation, i.e., a general, already-accepted pattern of succession).
Because of the contact of mind with the specific locus (in the soul) associated with a cognition, and because remembering arises from this, cognitions do not occur simultaneously.
(Objection): Not so, because mind operates (confined) within the body (so a soul-locus-contact model referring to something beyond the body seems unnecessary or unsupported).

Because this would itself require (independent) proof, it cannot be assumed as a basis here (i.e., the claim that mind is strictly confined to the body, used to reject the soul-locus account, is itself an unproven assumption).
For one who is remembering, the ongoing maintenance of the body itself is (perfectly) accounted for (on the Nyaya model, without contradiction), (so the objection's worry is unfounded).
(Objection continued): Not so, because mind (being atomic and swift) moves too rapidly (for its contact-based mechanism to be tracked or to explain memory in the orderly way claimed).

Not so, because there is no fixed rule regarding WHEN memory occurs (i.e., memory's evidently irregular, unpredictable timing is exactly what we'd expect from a swift-moving mind making variable contacts, not a problem for the account).

And this is not merely a matter of the soul's own effort (prerana), or of mere chance (yadrccha), or of automatic/inherent knowledge alone (accounting fully for when memories arise) -- (multiple distinct causal factors are involved).

It is comparable to a specific conjunction (occasioned) by pain in the foot, occurring even for someone whose mind is engaged elsewhere (i.e., an involuntary trigger can redirect mind's contact suddenly, illustrating how memory can arise unbidden).

Because the various kinds of knowledge involved -- (deliberate) attention, inferential marks, and so forth -- do not occur simultaneously, memory too does not arise simultaneously (with its various possible triggers, but one at a time, as each triggering condition comes into play).
Because the knowing agent's engagement in undertaking or ceasing (an action) is motivated by desire and aversion.

Because they (desire and aversion) are the marks/indicators of these (undertaking and ceasing), there is no valid objection (to positing them) even with regard to earthy and other (elemental substances lacking a soul, since desire/aversion mark ONLY ensouled beings, this actually confirms rather than threatens the soul's role).

In the case of iron and similar substances, we do observe (something resembling) undertaking and ceasing of activity (e.g. movement toward a magnet) -- (raising a possible complication for the desire/aversion criterion).
Rather, regularity and irregularity (of behavior) are what distinguish (the two cases, i.e., mere mechanical response from genuinely purposive, desire-driven action).

It is not (a quality) of mind, because of (mind's) dependence on the yet-to-be-established causal factors just discussed (desire, aversion etc.), its dependency on other agencies, and because it does not follow from unearned/unaccounted results (in the way ultimately required).
By elimination (parishesha), and because of the fitness/appropriateness of the previously stated reasons, (the soul is established as buddhi's true substrate).
Memory (properly) belongs to the soul, owing to the soul's inherent nature as a knower (jna-svabhavya).

(A comprehensive list of the causes/occasions of memory): from focused attention, association/linkage, repeated practice, an inferential sign, a defining characteristic, resemblance, a possessed object, that on which one is dependent or which depends on oneself, immediate succession, separation, a shared function, opposition, excess, receiving, intervention/obstruction, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, fear, a specific need/want, an action performed, and attachment or its opposite -- (from all of these), memory arises.

(Objection, reviving a worry from action/karma): Because of the perception of action (karma) as something unsteady/non-abiding (implying, by analogy, cognition too might be too fleeting to be properly 'grasped' as belonging to anything stable).
The grasping of something unmanifest/indistinct, owing to its transience, is like the grasping of the indistinct form (of an object) in a sudden flash of lightning.
By adopting the relevant governing principle (already established), the matter requiring rebuttal is (thereby) conceded/accounted for.

It is not (comparable) to the grasping of a lamp-flame's continuous series through its expressed/manifest appearance, (since cognition's case, while sharing some transience, has its own distinct explanatory basis already given).

There is doubt (as to which qualities belong to the substance itself versus qualities belonging to another substance combined with it), since we observe both a substance's own qualities and qualities of other substances (co-present) in it.
Because qualities such as colour persist as long as the body itself persists, (they might be considered inherent, permanent bodily qualities, by analogy raising the question for cognition too).

Not so, because of the arising of different qualities through cooking/heating (paka), (showing that even long-lasting bodily qualities like colour are actually produced/modifiable, not simply eternally inherent).

Because a stable state opposing (an original quality) can be established (through such processing), there is no valid objection to admitting these heat/processing-produced qualities (as a real, recognized category).

(Objection, reviving the case for treating cognition like a bodily quality): Because of its pervading the whole body, (cognition, like other bodily qualities, might be thought to characterize the body as a whole).

Not so, because it (cognition) is not apprehended in hair, nails, and similar (bodily) parts (unlike genuinely pervasive bodily qualities, which do extend to every part of the body without exception).
Because the body's (relevant, unifying) domain extends only up to the skin, there is no cognition-related issue arising in hair, nails, and the like (which lie beyond that living, sentient boundary).
Because of the essential dissimilarity (in the very manner cognition manifests) from (ordinary) bodily qualities, (cognition remains categorically distinct from qualities like colour).

(Objection): Not so, because of the mutual dissimilarity among qualities like colour themselves, (variety-among-bodily-qualities doesn't by itself prove cognition belongs to a wholly different category from them).

Not so, because (ordinary qualities like) colour and the rest, despite their mutual variety, remain uniformly perceptible by the (external) senses, (unlike cognition, which is apprehended in a fundamentally different, internal manner) -- so no valid objection stands.
(One view): There is a single mind, because of the non-simultaneity of cognitions.

(Objection): Not so, because we do observe the simultaneous occurrence of several distinct activities (e.g., a skilled person simultaneously seeing, hearing, and acting), (which a single mind operating strictly one-at-a-time could not explain).

The apprehension of that (apparent simultaneity) is like the perception of a (single) firebrand as a continuous circle of fire (when whirled rapidly) -- (an illusion of simultaneity produced by extremely swift sequential movement).
And because of the very reasons already stated (governing mind's nature and operation), mind is atomic (in size/extent).
(A new topic): The body arises in connection with (i.e., as a consequence of) the fruits/results of past actions (karma).
It (the body) is fashioned/composed from the elements, just as an embodied form is fashioned/taken up from them (in general, as already established for material composition).

(Objection): This (reliance on unseen karma as an explanation) is an unproved reason (sadhya-sama), (since karma's operation in producing embodiment is exactly the point requiring independent proof, not something to be assumed).

Not so, because of its role as a causal factor with respect to the parents (i.e., karma's operation is evidenced by its determining role in bringing specific parents together as the proximate cause of a given birth).
Likewise (karma plays a determining causal role) with respect to nourishment/sustenance (i.e., why a particular being's growth and sustenance unfolds as it does, tracking karmic factors).

And because there is no fixed rule regarding the mere attainment (of a body through elemental combination alone, without invoking karma, various anomalies in who is born how and where would otherwise go unexplained).
Just as the coming-together (of parents) that leads to formation of a body has its own determining cause, so karma constitutes the determining cause for a (particular soul's) conjunction/embodiment.
By this (established reasoning), the (earlier) objection regarding the absence of a fixed rule has already been answered.

(A further objection): If it be said that this (embodiment) is caused by unseen force/karma (adrshta) alone, (without further qualification), then the same problem would recur even with respect to final liberation (apavarga) -- (i.e., liberation too would then seem to require some further embodiment-producing karma, absurdly, undermining the possibility of a final release from the cycle).

And because of mind's role as the (proximate) causal factor for the (soul-body) conjunction (rather than karma alone acting automatically), there is no absolute severance (implied) of that conjunction (merely from the presence of residual, inert karmic seeds without an active proximate cause).

And this would (otherwise) entail the undesired consequence of the impossibility of dying, (since if karma alone, without needing mind's engagement, always necessitated immediate rebirth, there could be no gap -- no real 'death' as ordinarily understood -- between one embodiment and the next).

This might be compared to the fixed dark colour of an atom, (which persists as a stable, settled feature) -- (so too, one might think, embodiment-tendency could be a similarly fixed, permanent feature of karma).

Not so, because that would entail the undesired consequence of embodiment recurring even without any (further) unearned, appropriate karmic result (still awaiting fruition) -- (an absurd over-generation the resolving doctrine of mind's necessary role correctly avoids).
Activity (pravrtti) is exactly as it has been previously described.
Likewise, the faults (doshas) are (exactly as previously described).
Those (faults) form three distinct groups, because attachment (raga), aversion (dvesha), and delusion/ignorance (moha) are mutually distinct in their meaning/nature.
(Objection): No, because they (all three) have a single common opposite/antidote (namely, right knowledge, tatva-jnana -- implying they shouldn't be treated as fundamentally distinct).
This is not a valid reason, because it is overly broad/erratic (vyabhichara) (i.e., different diseases can sometimes share a single cure, so a shared antidote doesn't prove identity of the diseases).
Of these three, delusion (moha) is the worst/most pernicious, because the other two (attachment and aversion) do not arise in one who is free from delusion.

(A new topic: Transmigration): Because of the continuous, beginningless connection of cause (nimitta) and effect (naimittika) (i.e., past actions causing future births), (transmigration is established).

(Objection, from a materialist view): Not so, because we clearly observe the (purely physical/immediate) causes of origination and destruction (of bodies, without needing a beginningless karmic chain).

This is no valid objection, just as (observing immediate causes of destruction) does not negate the (underlying) non-eternality in things like colour (i.e., physical causes are only proximate; they don't explain the underlying pattern of necessity).

(A rival view - Shunyavada/Buddhist Emptiness): Void/Emptiness (shunya) is the material cause of all positive entities, because positive entities are seen to arise from non-existence (e.g., a sprout arises only when the seed is destroyed/ceases to exist).
(Nyaya Reply): Positive entities do not arise from non-existence; rather, they manifest by modifying/breaking down (the prior form of the material, not from absolute nothingness).
Because of self-contradiction, the expression (that things arise from non-existence) is unworkable.

(Objection attempting to defend Emptiness): Not so, because words denoting causal agents are routinely used with reference to past and future (i.e. currently non-existent) things (e.g. 'a son will be born', treating a non-existent thing as a subject).
(Nyaya Reply): This does not (save the theory that) positive entities arise from absolute non-existence.
(A second rival view - Absolute Theistic Determinism): God (Ishvara) alone is the (sole and sufficient) cause, because we observe that human effort often bears no fruit.
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because in the absence of human action (karma), the fruit (result) is not produced.
(Nyaya's own balanced Theistic position): This is not a valid objection (against God's role), because human action is itself actuated/supervised by Him (God).
(A third rival view - Accidentalism/Acausalism): Things are produced without any cause, just as things like space (akasha) and the like (are uncaused and simply exist).
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because (on that view) the observable relationship between cause and effect would be inexplicable.
(A fourth rival view - Universal Non-Eternality / Buddhism): Everything is non-eternal (transient), because everything possesses the properties of origination and destruction.
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because this very 'non-eternality' (if true of everything) would itself have to be eternal.

(Objection defending Universal Non-Eternality): That non-eternality (can apply to itself without paradox), just as fire, having burned everything else, is itself destroyed (by its own nature, without leaving anything eternal).

(Nyaya Reply): Because eternal things (like atoms, space, and souls) cannot be logically denied, the matter must be settled exactly as things are actually perceived (i.e., some things are eternal, some are non-eternal).
(A fifth rival view - Universal Eternality / Extreme Samkhya): Everything is eternal, because the five material elements (which make up everything) are eternal.
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because we clearly observe the causes of origination and destruction (of composite objects).

(Objection defending Universal Eternality): Because the fundamental characteristics of those (elements) remain present (even in the destroyed object), there is no valid denial (of their underlying eternality).
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because we clearly observe the causes of origination and destruction (reiterating that the WHOLE is distinct from its PARTS).
(A sixth rival view - Radical Pluralism/Atomism): Everything is entirely separate (and discrete), because the defining characteristics of all entities are utterly distinct from one another.
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because it is entirely possible/logical for a single entity to possess multiple distinct characteristics.
Because these distinct characteristics are established in a fixed, coordinated way (in the object), there is no valid denial (of the unified whole).

(A seventh rival view - Absolute Nihilism): Everything is non-existent (abhava), because the non-existence of one thing as another is established among all positive entities (e.g., a cow is 'not a horse').
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because positive entities are established by their own intrinsic nature (svabhava), (not merely by their difference from other things).
(Objection attempting to defend Nihilism/Relativism): There is no establishment of intrinsic nature, because everything is purely relative (e.g., 'long' only exists in relation to 'short').
(Nyaya Reply): This is illogical, because it is self-contradictory.

(Moving to the next topic): There is doubt (about the nature of karmic results/phala), because we observe results occurring both immediately (e.g. eating brings instant satisfaction) and at a later time (e.g. farming brings a harvest months later).
(Objection): There is no (delayed result), because results are only produced immediately, not at a later time (i.e., if it doesn't happen now, it wasn't caused by the action).

(Nyaya Reply): The occurrence of results at a later time is established by the analogy of the fruit of a tree (where watering the roots now produces fruit much later, through an unseen intermediate process).

(Objection questioning the ontological status of the 'result' before it happens): Not so, because prior to its origination, the result is completely non-existent (so how can it be 'aimed at' or 'caused' by the present action?).
And because, (if the result were somehow already existent before its manifestation), there could be no established order (of cause preceding effect).
(Nyaya Reply): There is no valid objection, because it is perfectly logical that a cause brings into existence what has not yet originated.
(Moving to the next topic): The origination of birth (i.e., embodied life) is nothing but suffering (duhkha), because it is invariably connected with various kinds of distress.
(Objection): Not so, because pleasure (sukha) is also produced in the intervals (between sufferings).
(Nyaya Reply): (We say it is all suffering) because worldly pleasures are deeply intertwined with distress; therefore, they are treated as (forms of) suffering.
And also because what people proudly consider 'pleasure' is often just a variation/interruption of suffering.
(Objection against the possibility of Moksha): There can be no Final Liberation (apavarga), because of the continuous binding force of debts (rna), afflictions (klesha), and activity (pravrtti).

(Nyaya Reply): Since the primary/literal meaning (of the word 'debt' here) is impossible, the statement is a secondary/figurative usage (guna-shabda), intended for the purpose of blame (for neglecting duties) and praise (for fulfilling them).
Because the (sacrificial fires) can be internalized (samaropana) within oneself, there is no valid denial (of the renouncer's path to liberation).
And this is also proven by the fact that the (requirement for ritual action) ends with the collection of the sacrificial vessels (at the cremation of a householder).
(The Nature of Liberation): Final Liberation (apavarga) is like the absence of all afflictions experienced by one in deep, dreamless sleep (sushupti).
(Objection): No (liberation is not possible), because the continuity of activity (pravrtti) is unbroken.
(Nyaya Reply): Final Liberation (apavarga) occurs due to the definitive cessation (apavarga) of the continuity of afflictions (klesha, namely delusion, attachment, and aversion).
Through the attainment of true knowledge (tatva-jnana) concerning the causes of the faults (doshas), the ego-sense (ahankara / false identification) ceases.
The causes of the faults are the objects of sense (colour, sound, etc.), which are constructed/magnified by mental resolve/imagination (sankalpa).
But the determination of the true nature of those (objects) is (essential); since the (false notion of the body as the) 'whole' (avayavin) is removed, the ego-sense ceases.

(Objection based on Buddhist Idealism/Nihilism): There is doubt (about whether this 'whole' exists at all even as an aggregate), because we must distinguish between true knowledge (vidya) and false knowledge (avidya).
(Nyaya Reply): There is no doubt about this, because the reasons previously stated (in Book 2, proving the reality of the Whole) are logically sound.
(Objection pressing the attack): But since the existence (of a whole residing in its parts) is logically impossible, there is indeed no doubt (i.e., it is certain the whole does NOT exist).
(Explaining the opponent's logic): Because the whole cannot reside in the parts either in its entirety (krtsna) or partially (eka-desha), the whole does not exist.
(Opponent continues): And because it does not reside in them (the parts), the whole does not exist.
(Opponent continues): And it does not exist separately from the parts (so it cannot be found anywhere else either).
(Opponent concludes): And the whole is certainly not (identical to) the parts (since 'one' is not 'many').
(Nyaya Reply): The objection is invalid, because terms implying division/difference ('entirety' or 'partially') cannot be applied to a single, unified entity, since it has no (inherent) divisions.
Even if there were no other parts, the argument that 'it does not reside' would be invalid.

(Buddhist Idealist Objection): The perception of that (apparent 'whole') is like the perception of a mass of hair by someone suffering from an eye disease (timira) (i.e., it is an optical illusion of a unified thing where there is only a loose aggregate).

(Nyaya Reply): A sense organ, whether sharp or dull, operates strictly within its own specific domain; it grasps its object accordingly, but it never operates on what is NOT its object (i.e., illusions are misinterpretations of real data, not hallucinations out of nothing).
(Furthermore, the opponent's view fails) because it relies on the impossibility, as well as the possibility, of the instruments of knowledge (pramanas) (which is self-contradictory).
(Note: this sutra text is sometimes considered a scribal repetition of the previous, but traditionally read as reinforcing the conclusion against idealism before moving on).
(Now establishing Atoms): There is an absence of that (i.e., the process of dividing things into smaller parts must come to an end), because there must be an absence of parts (at the ultimate level).
(Buddhist Objection): This (indivisible atom) is impossible, because ether/space (akasha) permeates it.
(Opponent continues): Or else, (if you claim the atom is solid and blocks space), you must admit that ether/space is not all-pervading (which contradicts your own Nyaya tenets).
(Nyaya Reply): This is a false argument, because the terms 'inside' and 'outside' are applicable only to (composite) products, not to simple substances.
And also because sound and conjunction are produced (everywhere, proving space is all-pervading, without contradicting the solidity of atoms).
Because there is no arrangement/composition (vyuha) in an atom, it has no parts.

(Objection, from Vijnanavada / Subjective Idealism): (Even if atoms existed), the perception of form/shape is justified (purely as a mental projection, like a dream), because it appears as having limited corporeal form.
(Nyaya Reply): (This view fails) because it relies on the impossibility, as well as the possibility, of the instruments of knowledge (pramanas).
(Idealist Objection): The notion of 'instruments of knowledge' and 'objects of knowledge' is just a false conceit, exactly like the notion of objects seen in a dream.
(Nyaya Reply): The false conceit of objects in a dream is actually similar to memory and imagination (which require prior waking experience of real things).
The destruction of false apprehension occurs through True Knowledge (tatva-jnana), just as the false conceit of dream-objects is destroyed upon waking up.

(Objection regarding the maintenance of knowledge): (If true knowledge is just a cognition), it is an invalid means (to eternal liberation), because cognitions are subject to arising and disappearing (so the knowledge will fade and bondage will return).
(Nyaya Reply): (True Knowledge is maintained and deepened) through the continuous practice (abhyasa) of a specific form of meditative concentration (samadhi).
(Objection): No (meditation won't work), because of the overwhelming power of specific external sense-objects (which will forcibly break the meditator's concentration).
(Objection continues): And also because a person is forcibly driven to act by hunger, thirst, and the like.
(Nyaya Reply): That (distraction by hunger or objects) occurs as a consequence of the fruits of past actions (karma) (and is precisely what the practice is designed to eventually exhaust).
Hence the injunction to practice Yoga (meditation) in forests, caves, and on sandy riverbanks (to minimize external distractions).
(Objection): If (liberation requires this constant effort), then the same necessity (for effort) would apply even in the state of Final Liberation (making it not true liberation).
(Nyaya Reply): Not so, because (Liberation) is an accomplished/final state (where all bodies and senses have fallen away).
In Liberation, there is an absence of that (distraction and effort), because of the complete absence of the afflictions (kleshas).

For the sake of that (attaining liberation), one must practice self-restraint (Yama), observances (Niyama), and the purification of the soul (atma-samskara) by means of the spiritual methods and rules prescribed in Yoga.
One should engage in the repeated study/grasping of (philosophical) knowledge, and hold discussions (samvada) with those who possess that knowledge.
One should approach such discussions with disciples, teachers, fellow-students, and other distinguished seekers of the highest good, who are free from malice/envy (anasuyu).
Or, if one is a seeker of truth, one may engage in discussion even without holding a strictly opposing view (just for the purpose of clarification).
But Disputation (Jalpa) and Wrangling (Vitanda) may be used for the purpose of protecting one's determination of truth, just as a fence of thorny branches is used to protect the sprouting of a seed.
Engaging in quarrelsome/combative debate is done by means of those two (Jalpa and Vitanda).
This is for the purpose of subduing the arrogance/glory (tejas) of an aggressive opponent.

properties.context: Yoga collapses the Antahkarana into Citta
